author: NTD
title: DOJ: States Must Report Illegal Immigrants or Risk Welfare Funds
text:
The U.S. Justice Department has warned that states could lose billions of dollars in welfare funding if they do not report known illegal immigrants.
statementsaying it revised a legal opinion in relation to illegal immigrants, where all agencies in states participating in two federal public assistance programs must report all immigrants who are in the country illegally or risk losing program funding.
The revised opinion applies to states receiving Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) funds and those operating under certain Supplemental Security Income (SSI) agreements. Previously, the federal government required reports only from the state offices directly administering those programs.
accordingto the Sept. 1 legal opinion from the department’s Office of Legal Counsel.
accordingto the Department of Health and Human Services.
accordingto the Social Security Administration (SSA).
Federal lawrequires states participating in the TANF program to submit to the Department of Homeland Security the names, addresses, and other identifying information of individuals known to be unlawfully present in the U.S., and to file these reports at least four times per year or when requested by federal authorities.
Deputy Assistant Attorney General Joshua Craddock, who wrote the opinion, said the department was restoring what it considers the original meaning of the law, not creating a new obligation.
“States that accept TANF funding must abide by federal law, and failure to comply may lead to serious consequences, including loss of program funding,” he said.
Assistant Attorney General T. Elliot Gaiser said Congress made reporting a condition of state participation in TANF. He said the requirement was intended to reinforce federal immigration law.
Previous Interpretation Narrowed Reporting Requirements
In the DOJ opinion, which is not law but is binding on federal agencies, Craddock said the previous interpretation, issued in 1998, wrongly narrowed the scope of the 1996 Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act by using the word "State" to mean a specific state agency, rather than every agency in a state government.The 1998 opinion from the Office of Legal Counsel previously limited the reporting obligation to agencies that directly administered TANF or SSI. That interpretation was withdrawn in the Sept. 1 legal opinion, which clarified that the term “State” refers to the entire state government and all of its agencies.
The updated opinion also broadens the definition of when a state agency “knows” someone is unlawfully present. Under a 2000 federal notice, a formal finding by immigration authorities—such as a final deportation order—was typically required.
The Justice Department now says a formal removal order is not always necessary. An agency may have sufficient knowledge based on Department of Homeland Security records, expired immigration documents, or an individual’s own admission that they entered unlawfully and lack a legal basis to remain.
Federal TANF grants exceed $16.4 billion annually, and SSI federal benefits exceed $60 billion annually. Immigrants without legal status are not eligible for either program.
States could have knowledge of millions of people without legal immigration status inside their borders—at least 19 states, including Washington, allow immigrants without lawful status to obtain driver’s licenses, while many state universities also admit such students.

The revised opinion applies to states receiving Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) funds and those operating under certain Supplemental Security Income (SSI) agreements. Deputy Assistant Attorney General Joshua Craddock, who wrote the opinion, said the department was restoring what it considers the original meaning of the law, not creating a new obligation. Assistant Attorney General T. Elliot Gaiser said Congress made reporting a condition of state participation in TANF.
